leads_to.evidence: BLS says entry-level mechanical engineers need a bachelor's degree but no license. Graduates can take the FE exam right away, and a Professional Engineer license usually comes later in a career and is optional for many jobs.

nearby_pair.evidence: Both programs are four-year, ABET-accredited mechanical engineering degrees that admit first-year students. City College admits them through its engineering school from high school, and Manhattan University starts them in a common first-year engineering curriculum.

school_matters.evidence: Employers hire entry-level mechanical engineers on an accredited bachelor's degree, and no license is needed at the start. The degree itself opens the job market, which helps explain why pay at open schools runs close to pay at the most selective ones.

who_is_counted.evidence: None of the largest programs are online-only. Mechanical engineering programs admit freshmen who are ready for calculus into a four-year sequence, so graduates are mostly traditional new graduates and not working adults finishing a degree.

programs.evidence: Cal Maritime's mechanical engineering license track includes sea terms and the Coast Guard Third Assistant Engineer exam, so many graduates leave as licensed marine engineers who work aboard ships.
MIT admits a very small share of applicants, and its mechanical engineering graduates are recruited by top technology, research and finance employers.
Penn admits a very small share of applicants, and its mechanical engineering graduates are recruited by top employers, consulting firms included.
More than half of VMI graduates are commissioned as military officers. They start in service at junior-officer pay, much of it in untaxed allowances, instead of taking civilian engineering jobs.
Norwich is a senior military college that produces many ROTC officers each year. Many of its engineering graduates enter military service instead of civilian engineering jobs.
This campus is in Puerto Rico, where engineering pay sits well below mainland levels.
